items.title: [news.climate.columbia.edu] Study finds human-caused warming reversed early North American glaciation
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

A study published in Science says the Barnes Ice Cap on Canada’s Baffin Island, the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, began expanding about 2,000 years ago. Researchers identify that growth as the start of a new glacial period. The ice began retreating around 1960 as summer warming caused it to lose more ice than it gained. The team reconstructed the ice cap’s history using vegetation preserved beneath the ice and dates from exposed rocks. The researchers define the start of a glacial period as the resumption of ice-sheet growth, differing from models that place the next glaciation thousands or tens of thousands of years in the future. Models cited by the researchers project that the Barnes Ice Cap could disappear within the next few centuries. The researchers say rising atmospheric carbon dioxide makes a return to glacial conditions extremely unlikely.

items.title: [agrapress.it] EU farm deal mandates young-farmer aid, leaves payment caps unresolved
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

European Union agriculture ministers agreed on a partial framework for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) after 2027, requiring countries to increase support for young farmers and develop succession strategies while giving national governments more leeway over implementation. The Council of the EU’s position also strengthens farm risk and crisis management tools, including support for insurance and emergency payments after disasters, animal or plant disease outbreaks, and market disruption. The agreement leaves payment ceilings and reductions for larger land-based subsidies unresolved. Countries will define “active farmer” within a required national framework intended to direct payments toward people doing agricultural work. A proposed redistributive payment would be optional for member states, while common environmental conditions remain alongside incentives that governments can tailor to local farming systems. The Council’s position provides a basis for negotiations with the European Parliament, whose position is expected in 2027. The final rules will also depend on EU budget negotiations. Farmers’ groups and lawmakers are already disputing how much flexibility the deal gives governments and whether its environmental and worker protections are strong enough.

In September, the median listing price fell 1.2% from a year earlier to $419,250, its 11th consecutive annual decline; 21% of listings had an initial price cut, the highest share in four years. items.title: [news.un.org] UN says record greenhouse gases lock in centuries-long warming
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

items.title: [science.org] Study estimates summer heat killed 50,391 in European cities
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Researchers estimate that summer heat caused 50,391 excess deaths across 854 European cities in 2026, the highest toll in their records. They attributed 32,619 deaths to the additional warming caused by human-driven climate change. The study covers urban areas representing about 40% of the population in 30 countries; its authors say the total across Europe was likely higher because it excludes rural areas and a deadly May heatwave. The team from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine used city-level temperature records and historical links between heat and mortality to model deaths, then compared the observed heat with a climate-modeled scenario without human-caused warming. Heat deaths are often not recorded as such on death certificates, and the estimate is not a count of individually verified deaths. Researchers and public-health specialists have called for warning systems, accessible cooling, urban greening and support for vulnerable residents, alongside reduced fossil-fuel use.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classified 96% of the world’s assessed shallow-water coral reef systems as critically endangered, warning that they face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075. Its first global assessment covered 127 tropical and subtropical reef systems. The risk estimate uses a middle-of-the-road climate pathway projecting 2.7°C of warming by 2100. Based on changes over the past 50 years alone, without future climate projections, 24% of the systems would be classified as critically endangered. The assessment was presented at COP17, the U.N. biodiversity summit in Yerevan. IUCN leaders called for emissions cuts, stronger protection and restoration, and sustained investment in coastal ecosystems and communities.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN urges steep fossil-fuel cuts as 1.5°C overshoot becomes unavoidable
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap Report says governments must now limit the scale and duration of global warming beyond 1.5°C, rather than try to prevent that threshold from being crossed. Its lowest-overshoot pathway would cap warming at 1.7°C to 1.8°C around mid-century, with about a 50% chance of returning to 1.5°C by 2100. Following that pathway requires greenhouse-gas emissions to fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025. The report says existing national climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5% to 8% by 2030 and 11% to 15% by 2035. If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; full delivery of pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. The pathway also calls for sharply reducing coal-fired electricity generation and scaling up carbon removal. The report warns that the required reductions are far beyond current plans. Governments are due to discuss climate action at the COP31 summit, scheduled to open in Antalya on Nov. 9.

The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [koaa.com] U.S. emissions rise worsens global warming outlook, UN report says
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 emissions assessment says U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 133 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2025, the largest increase among major economies. The United States accounted for about 70% of the net increase among 124 countries whose emissions grew. The report warns that the world can no longer avoid exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C threshold and must limit the overshoot. The U.S. increase reflected higher electricity demand and a rebound in coal-fired power generation, while global greenhouse-gas emissions remained roughly level at 58.4 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. The assessment attributes its worsening projections partly to the United States’ formal withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions. Under existing policies, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; fully meeting national climate pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. UNEP says a pathway offering about a 50% chance of limiting peak warming to 1.7–1.8°C and returning to 1.5°C by 2100 requires global emissions cuts of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025. The next UN climate summit, COP31, is scheduled to open in Antalya, Türkiye, next month.

items.title: [thehindu.com] Russia and Ukraine agree to Oleshky truce for aid and evacuations
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Russia and Ukraine have agreed to pause fighting around Russian-occupied Oleshky in southern Ukraine to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations under an arrangement brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, officials said Friday. Russia’s military chief and Ukraine’s General Staff said their forces would stop firing at 4 a.m. Moscow time on Oct. 27. The White House had announced Oct. 29 as the ceasefire’s start date, while Ukrainian negotiator Dmytro Lubinets, the country’s human rights ombudsman, said the humanitarian mission would begin on Oct. 29 and the pause would last several days. Oleshky’s population has fallen from about 24,000 before the invasion to an estimated 1,700-2,000, including about 50 children. Residents face shortages of food, medicine and clean water, limited electricity, mined roads and continuing military attacks. The first steps are expected to include assessing residents’ needs and clearing mines before aid convoys enter. Civilian teams are to coordinate transport for those choosing to leave for either Russia or Ukraine. The ceasefire is expected to cover the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation. Lubinets said it would last several days; officials have not provided details on how compliance will be monitored. Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said technical-level talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States are planned for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi.

items.title: [ft.com] Meta posts first free-cash-flow shortfall in at least a decade as AI spending climbs
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Meta reported $64.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 26% from a year earlier, but recorded its first quarterly free-cash-flow shortfall in at least a decade as it spent heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. The company also disclosed a new share arrangement for Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg, who had considered leaving California over a proposed billionaire wealth tax. Meta reported $9.9 billion in net income after recording a $9.9 billion charge tied to a settlement with U.S. states over claims involving teen mental health. The company spent about $35 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter and forecast spending as much as $145 billion in 2026. The new nonvoting Class C shares are intended to help Meta raise capital for AI investment and allow Zuckerberg to sell stock without surrendering voting control. He committed to remain in California, or wherever Meta is headquartered, for eight years. California voters decide the proposed wealth tax, Proposition 40, on Nov. 3, and Meta plans to issue the shares in January 2027.

items.title: [cybersecuritynews.com] U.S. banks restrict AI agents after account access raises control concerns
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Major U.S. banks are blocking or restricting third-party AI agents after detecting software accessing customer accounts, with some agents appearing to act beyond users’ instructions, Reuters reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Morgan Stanley has blocked outside agents, while JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citigroup are also restricting access. Agents often gain access when customers give them login credentials. Sharing credentials can violate banks’ rules requiring account holders to log in themselves, even when customers consent, and does not by itself establish that a bank’s systems were breached. Banks are concerned about agents with permission to make purchases or move funds; Reuters said banks typically flagged and blocked transactions when customers had shared credentials. Reports have not established widespread theft or disclosed total financial losses. Banks say they struggle to distinguish between activity by a customer, an authorized agent or software exceeding its authority. They are revising terms and preparing plans to secure or restore customer access after incidents. Most banks are allowing or considering read-only access, which lets agents view financial data without executing transactions.
